Ken Faulkner (who played for Birmingham City in the 1940s) was a member of **Birmingham City** – the club that last defeated the league’s 1894‑95 FA Cup winner, Aston Villa, on **20 March 2005** when the Blues won 2–0 at St Andrew’s.  

*Source:* Wikipedia, “Second City derby” – “The last Birmingham City league victory over Aston Villa was on 20 March 2005, when Blues won 2‑0 at St Andrew's.” (【10†L14-L17】)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
**Kenneth William Faulkner** (born 1948) is a former Republican Party politician who served for 10 weeks in the New Jersey General Assembly. After a collegiate career with the Campbell Fighting Camels basketball team, he was inducted into the Campbell University Hall of Fame.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-1) He is also a retired teacher, school administrator and high school basketball coach.
Faulkner grew up in Delanco Township, New Jersey and graduated from Riverside High School as part of the class of 1966. After playing at Campbell College (now Campbell University), he became a high school basketball coach. During his 24-year coaching career at Burlington Township High School, Faulkner led the team to a 521–129 record and three NJSIAA Group I state championships. He stepped down from his position as coach in 1996 to take a post as principal of Thomas O. Hopkins Middle School, stating that he couldn't be both a basketball coach and an effective school administrator.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-2)
Faulkner, a resident of Delanco Township, was chosen to replace Carmine DeSopo on the Republican ticket for the [7th Legislative District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey's_7th_legislative_district "New Jersey's 7th legislative district"), together with George Williams running for the other Assembly seat and Diane Allen for Senate.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-3)

In the November 1997 general elections, Allen won the Senate seat, while Democrats Herb Conaway and Jack Conners were declared the winners in that year's Assembly race, after a recount which showed that Conaway was the top vote-getter and Conners winning the second seat by a margin of 74 votes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-4) In September 1998, the New Jersey Superior Court threw out the results of the 1997 election due to problems with 160 uncounted ballots from a voting machine that affected the results for the second seat; Democrat Conners was ordered to leave office and Republican Faulkner was seated in his place.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-5)
The Republican committees of Burlington County and Camden County chose Faulkner to fill the vacated Assembly seat and the ballot position for the forthcoming special election; After being sworn into office on September 18, Faulkner used his first day in office to co-sponsor a bill raising awareness regarding arthritis, in addition to working to address issues related to education, healthcare and property taxes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-6)
In a November 1998 special election held based on the court order throwing out the 1997 election results, Conners defeated Faulkner by 5,500 votes and was sworn into office on November 23 for the second time that year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-8)

"During Faulkner's 24 seasons of coaching at Burlington Township, the Falcons compiled a 521-129 record and won 13 division titles, seven sectional crowns, and three Group 1 state championships (1985, 1987, 1992).... A former star guard at Riverside High (Class of '66) and Campbell (N.C. 1970) College, Faulkner knew that he was going to retire before this season started."  
3.   ↑Mulvihill, Geoff. "Principal Is Tapped To Run For Assembly Ken Faulkner, A Burlington Twp. "Ken Faulkner, a middle school principal in Burlington Township, yesterday won key endorsements to replace Carmine DeSopo as a Republican candidate for State Assembly from the Seventh District. # Campbell University
## Ken Faulkner
*   Class 1970  
*   Induction 1999  
*   Sport(s)Men's Basketball
**Tales from the Creek Podcast | Ken Faulkner (January 2026)**
Ken Faulkner was inducted into the Campbell Athletics Hall of Fame in 1999. A guard on some of Campbell's finest basketball teams in the late 1960s, Faulkner went on to become one of the greatest coaches in New Jersey high school basketball history.
Faulkner was a four-year starter for Coach Fred McCall's and Coach Danny Roberts' Fighting Camels. During his junior and senior years, he helped the club to back-to-back 20-win seasons and NAIA District 29 championships.
In 1970, the Camels won 24 games and advanced to the NAIA National Tournament.
Following graduation in 1970, Faulkner returned to his native New Jersey and began a teaching and coaching career. He was named varsity boys basketball coach at Burlington Township High School and went on to build one of the premier programs in the state. In 24 seasons as a head coach, Faulkner's clubs won 522 games, 11 conference titles, seven South Jersey crowns and three state championships. His 1987 team posted a 31-0 record and is still considered one of the greatest teams in South Jersey basketball history.
Faulkner received numerous honors during his career. He was inducted into the Riverside High School, South Jersey Coaches, New Jersey Coaches and Basketball Club of South Jersey Halls of Fame. He was also presented the New Jersey Interscholastic Coaches Association's Honor Award.
Faulkner, who retired from coaching in 1996, later served in the New Jersey General Assembly.

Ken Faulkner arrived in Buies Creek from South Jersey in the summer of 1966 as a standout guard for Coach Fred McCall's Fighting Camel basketball team. By the time he graduated in 1970, he was not only a four-year starter but also helped lead his teams to back-to-back 20-win seasons and district titles. Following graduation, Ken returned to his native New Jersey and began a teaching and coaching career. At Burlington Township High School, he built one of the premier programs in the state. # Campbell University
## Ken Faulkner
*   Class 1970  
*   Induction 1999  
*   Sport(s)Men's Basketball
**Tales from the Creek Podcast | Ken Faulkner (January 2026)**
Ken Faulkner was inducted into the Campbell Athletics Hall of Fame in 1999. A guard on some of Campbell's finest basketball teams in the late 1960s, Faulkner went on to become one of the greatest coaches in New Jersey high school basketball history.
Faulkner was a four-year starter for Coach Fred McCall's and Coach Danny Roberts' Fighting Camels. During his junior and senior years, he helped the club to back-to-back 20-win seasons and NAIA District 29 championships.
In 1970, the Camels won 24 games and advanced to the NAIA National Tournament.
Following graduation in 1970, Faulkner returned to his native New Jersey and began a teaching and coaching career. He was named varsity boys basketball coach at Burlington Township High School and went on to build one of the premier programs in the state. In 24 seasons as a head coach, Faulkner's clubs won 522 games, 11 conference titles, seven South Jersey crowns and three state championships. His 1987 team posted a 31-0 record and is still considered one of the greatest teams in South Jersey basketball history.
Faulkner received numerous honors during his career. He was inducted into the Riverside High School, South Jersey Coaches, New Jersey Coaches and Basketball Club of South Jersey Halls of Fame. He was also presented the New Jersey Interscholastic Coaches Association's Honor Award.
Faulkner, who retired from coaching in 1996, later served in the New Jersey General Assembly.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
**Kenneth William Faulkner** (born 1948) is a former Republican Party politician who served for 10 weeks in the New Jersey General Assembly. After a collegiate career with the Campbell Fighting Camels basketball team, he was inducted into the Campbell University Hall of Fame.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-1) He is also a retired teacher, school administrator and high school basketball coach.
Faulkner grew up in Delanco Township, New Jersey and graduated from Riverside High School as part of the class of 1966. After playing at Campbell College (now Campbell University), he became a high school basketball coach. During his 24-year coaching career at Burlington Township High School, Faulkner led the team to a 521–129 record and three NJSIAA Group I state championships. He stepped down from his position as coach in 1996 to take a post as principal of Thomas O. Hopkins Middle School, stating that he couldn't be both a basketball coach and an effective school administrator.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-2)
Faulkner, a resident of Delanco Township, was chosen to replace Carmine DeSopo on the Republican ticket for the [7th Legislative District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey's_7th_legislative_district "New Jersey's 7th legislative district"), together with George Williams running for the other Assembly seat and Diane Allen for Senate.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-3)
texts.1:
In the November 1997 general elections, Allen won the Senate seat, while Democrats Herb Conaway and Jack Conners were declared the winners in that year's Assembly race, after a recount which showed that Conaway was the top vote-getter and Conners winning the second seat by a margin of 74 votes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-4) In September 1998, the New Jersey Superior Court threw out the results of the 1997 election due to problems with 160 uncounted ballots from a voting machine that affected the results for the second seat; Democrat Conners was ordered to leave office and Republican Faulkner was seated in his place.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-5)
The Republican committees of Burlington County and Camden County chose Faulkner to fill the vacated Assembly seat and the ballot position for the forthcoming special election; After being sworn into office on September 18, Faulkner used his first day in office to co-sponsor a bill raising awareness regarding arthritis, in addition to working to address issues related to education, healthcare and property taxes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-6)
In a November 1998 special election held based on the court order throwing out the 1997 election results, Conners defeated Faulkner by 5,500 votes and was sworn into office on November 23 for the second time that year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-8)

### Biography
After 34 years of following players and plays up and down football fields, blowing whistles and calling penalties, Ken Faulkner finally hung up his stripes for the last time on November 27, 1982. The game was Rice vs. Houston, two of his native state favorites. It was while working that game that Faulkner broke his ankle.
That injury, 12 years ago, took him off the field, but not away from college football. He still had his other love, serving as business manager of the Southwest Conference. When he finally retired in 1991, he also stepped down as SWC supervisor of football officials, a responsibility he handled for eight years.
When it comes to football, Ken Faulkner's dedication and devotion have made him a true "Legend of the Southwest" in officiating circles. Ask his SWC colleagues. To a man they'll tell you Faulkner made "a great impact on every football person he has ever worked with. He attracted enormous respect".
That respect has brought him recognition from the entire amateur football community and today he is honored by the National Football Foundation for his many years of work and contributions to the game.
Last year, Faulkner was similarly honored by the Collegiate Commissioners Association which presented him with its 1993 Football Officials Award of Merit.
During Faulkner's tenure as business manager, the Southwest Conference enjoyed a period of growth and athletic success unparalleled in the Conference's history. He oversaw distribution of Conference revenues for its nine member institutions which had combined to win 40 NCAA championships in 12 different sports during his nine-year watch. He managed $9 million annually for the SWC while, at the same time, supervising a crew of 40 officials.
Faulkner officiated his first football game while he was himself still a college student at what is today known as Mideastern State in Wichita Falls, Texas.
Faulkner said, "I discovered it was fun, something I really enjoyed." So he kept on doing it, even after he graduated with his bachelor's degree in physical education in 1950. Faulkner then got a job working for a freight company. But he kept those stripes and cleats clean for the weekend.

### Biography
As he progressed in his professional life, he was also stepping up on the gridiron. From officiating small college games, he graduated to larger ones and, finally, he was working major college games, some of the biggest games college football offered.
Among the Bowl Games Faulkner worked were the Orange, Sugar and Fiesta. He also regularly officiated one of college football's great rivalries, Texas versus Oklahoma.
In his off-the-field pursuits, Faulkner was a very successful major corporation internal auditor for 25 years. Then, in 1982, he joined the Southwest Conference as business manager. For Faulkner it was a perfect union of professional and personal pleasure.
Faulkner also became very involved in the work of the Collegiate Commissioners Association. For eight years he headed the CCA group that drafted and published officiating guidelines for the country's more than 10,000 college football officials.
These manuals deal with the mechanics of the job. "They tell the official everything he has to do from the time he gets out of his car at the stadium to the time he gets back home," says Faulkner. In addition to writing and producing the guidelines, Faulkner organized the distribution system to get them out to the officials all across the nation.
"That was midnight oil stuff," he says, "in addition to my duties with the Conference." And with no small amount of pride, he adds, "The system I set up is still in effect today."
Even though he officially retired in 1991, Faulkner is still involved in football. One of the things he does is scout college games, assessing officials who might be candidates to work for the National Football League.

*   Sport(s)Men's Basketball
**Tales from the Creek Podcast | Ken Faulkner (January 2026)**
Ken Faulkner was inducted into the Campbell Athletics Hall of Fame in 1999. A guard on some of Campbell's finest basketball teams in the late 1960s, Faulkner went on to become one of the greatest coaches in New Jersey high school basketball history.
Faulkner was a four-year starter for Coach Fred McCall's and Coach Danny Roberts' Fighting Camels. During his junior and senior years, he helped the club to back-to-back 20-win seasons and NAIA District 29 championships.
In 1970, the Camels won 24 games and advanced to the NAIA National Tournament.
Following graduation in 1970, Faulkner returned to his native New Jersey and began a teaching and coaching career. He was named varsity boys basketball coach at Burlington Township High School and went on to build one of the premier programs in the state. In 24 seasons as a head coach, Faulkner's clubs won 522 games, 11 conference titles, seven South Jersey crowns and three state championships. His 1987 team posted a 31-0 record and is still considered one of the greatest teams in South Jersey basketball history.
Faulkner received numerous honors during his career. He was inducted into the Riverside High School, South Jersey Coaches, New Jersey Coaches and Basketball Club of South Jersey Halls of Fame. He was also presented the New Jersey Interscholastic Coaches Association's Honor Award.
Faulkner, who retired from coaching in 1996, later served in the New Jersey General Assembly.

Meet the Teacher: Ken Faulkner
Ken Faulkner teaches Government and American History to juniors and seniors at Vista Grande High School.
Mr. Faulkner is celebrating 20 years in education. Originally from Los Angeles, he has been an Arizona resident since 2006 and an Arizona educator since 2008. Before joining Vista Grande in 2022, he spent 15 years teaching at an alternative school in Mesa. Prior to becoming a teacher, he had careers in pharmaceutical sales and even professional poker! He and his wife are raising three children and call Mesa home.
Why did you become a teacher?
"I wanted to contribute to society and my community."
Favorite book: Guns, Germs, and Steel by Jared Diamond
Favorite drink: McDonald's Iced Coffee
Favorite snack: Chocolate—in any form!
Favorite artist/song: The Ramones – Blitzkrieg Bop
Dream vacation: Japan
Favorite animal: Dogs
Favorite movie & TV show: Jaws and Seinfeld
Fun fact: He played college basketball and volleyball!
One thing he hopes every student learns:
"I hope my students learn how to be successful in life by being present, prepared, and engaged in their high school education."

# Campbell University
## Ken Faulkner
*   Class 1970  
*   Induction 1999  
*   Sport(s)Men's Basketball
**Tales from the Creek Podcast | Ken Faulkner (January 2026)**
Ken Faulkner was inducted into the Campbell Athletics Hall of Fame in 1999. A guard on some of Campbell's finest basketball teams in the late 1960s, Faulkner went on to become one of the greatest coaches in New Jersey high school basketball history.
Faulkner was a four-year starter for Coach Fred McCall's and Coach Danny Roberts' Fighting Camels. During his junior and senior years, he helped the club to back-to-back 20-win seasons and NAIA District 29 championships.
In 1970, the Camels won 24 games and advanced to the NAIA National Tournament.
Following graduation in 1970, Faulkner returned to his native New Jersey and began a teaching and coaching career. He was named varsity boys basketball coach at Burlington Township High School and went on to build one of the premier programs in the state. In 24 seasons as a head coach, Faulkner's clubs won 522 games, 11 conference titles, seven South Jersey crowns and three state championships. His 1987 team posted a 31-0 record and is still considered one of the greatest teams in South Jersey basketball history.
Faulkner received numerous honors during his career. He was inducted into the Riverside High School, South Jersey Coaches, New Jersey Coaches and Basketball Club of South Jersey Halls of Fame. He was also presented the New Jersey Interscholastic Coaches Association's Honor Award.
Faulkner, who retired from coaching in 1996, later served in the New Jersey General Assembly.

### Biography
After 34 years of following players and plays up and down football fields, blowing whistles and calling penalties, Ken Faulkner finally hung up his stripes for the last time on November 27, 1982. The game was Rice vs. Houston, two of his native state favorites. It was while working that game that Faulkner broke his ankle.
That injury, 12 years ago, took him off the field, but not away from college football. He still had his other love, serving as business manager of the Southwest Conference. When he finally retired in 1991, he also stepped down as SWC supervisor of football officials, a responsibility he handled for eight years.
When it comes to football, Ken Faulkner's dedication and devotion have made him a true "Legend of the Southwest" in officiating circles. Ask his SWC colleagues. To a man they'll tell you Faulkner made "a great impact on every football person he has ever worked with. He attracted enormous respect".
That respect has brought him recognition from the entire amateur football community and today he is honored by the National Football Foundation for his many years of work and contributions to the game.
Last year, Faulkner was similarly honored by the Collegiate Commissioners Association which presented him with its 1993 Football Officials Award of Merit.
During Faulkner's tenure as business manager, the Southwest Conference enjoyed a period of growth and athletic success unparalleled in the Conference's history. He oversaw distribution of Conference revenues for its nine member institutions which had combined to win 40 NCAA championships in 12 different sports during his nine-year watch. He managed $9 million annually for the SWC while, at the same time, supervising a crew of 40 officials.
Faulkner officiated his first football game while he was himself still a college student at what is today known as Mideastern State in Wichita Falls, Texas.
Faulkner said, "I discovered it was fun, something I really enjoyed." So he kept on doing it, even after he graduated with his bachelor's degree in physical education in 1950. Faulkner then got a job working for a freight company. But he kept those stripes and cleats clean for the weekend.
texts.1:
### Biography
As he progressed in his professional life, he was also stepping up on the gridiron. From officiating small college games, he graduated to larger ones and, finally, he was working major college games, some of the biggest games college football offered.
Among the Bowl Games Faulkner worked were the Orange, Sugar and Fiesta. He also regularly officiated one of college football's great rivalries, Texas versus Oklahoma.
In his off-the-field pursuits, Faulkner was a very successful major corporation internal auditor for 25 years. Then, in 1982, he joined the Southwest Conference as business manager. For Faulkner it was a perfect union of professional and personal pleasure.
Faulkner also became very involved in the work of the Collegiate Commissioners Association. For eight years he headed the CCA group that drafted and published officiating guidelines for the country's more than 10,000 college football officials.
These manuals deal with the mechanics of the job. "They tell the official everything he has to do from the time he gets out of his car at the stadium to the time he gets back home," says Faulkner. In addition to writing and producing the guidelines, Faulkner organized the distribution system to get them out to the officials all across the nation.
"That was midnight oil stuff," he says, "in addition to my duties with the Conference." And with no small amount of pride, he adds, "The system I set up is still in effect today."
Even though he officially retired in 1991, Faulkner is still involved in football. One of the things he does is scout college games, assessing officials who might be candidates to work for the National Football League.

Source: https://www.ot-campings.com/l-actualite/camping/le-retour-des-anglais/
Title: Le retour des anglais
Chunks: 0,1,2
L’été dernier, la crise financière conjuguée avec une chute de la valeur de la livre face à l’euro avait incité les Britanniques à rester chez eux pour les vacances.
L’été dernier, la crise financière conjuguée avec une chute de la valeur de la livre face à l’euro avait incité les Britanniques à rester chez eux pour les vacances.
Les premiers indicateurs de ce début d’année semblaient toutefois annoncer un regain d’intérêt de la clientèle anglaise pour les destinations continentales, et notamment françaises. Le Salon de la caravane qui s’est tenu fin février à Birmingham était une occasion de prendre la température du marché et de voir si ces espoirs allaient se concrétiser.
Avec **seulement 84 000 visiteurs**, soit les plus mauvais résultats de ces dernières années, la fréquentation du salon qui se tenait au National Exhibition Centre de Birmingham fut assez décevante au regard des précédentes éditions. Quelques journées en particulier furent jugées très calmes par les habitués du salon. On ne saurait toutefois pas imputer cette baisse du nombre d’entrées à un désintérêt de la clientèle britannique pour le camping. Le salon s’est en effet tenu une semaine plus tard que l’an passé et ne coïncidait donc pas avec les vacances scolaires anglaises et la météo n’a pas aidé à mobiliser les foules, avec de la neige les premiers jours et l’avis de tempête du 28 février pour la dernière journée. Si l’on ajoute à cela que la participation d’Aston Villa, club de football de Birmingham, à la finale de Coupe de la Ligue le dimanche après-midi aura retenu nombre de visiteurs potentiels devant la télévision, il faut admettre que la légère baisse de fréquentation du salon ne reflète pas du tout la popularité du camping chez nos voisins d’outre-Manche.

La **grande question**pour les campings français était de savoir si les clients anglais allaient retrouver le chemin de la France après l’avoir boudée l’été dernier. Le salon de la caravane de Birmingham qui se tient en octobre avait donné des signes encourageants qui demandaient à être confirmés. Et ce fut le cas. Les visiteurs du salon ont montré une réelle envie de venir en France. Et si la tendance 2009 était de ne pas partir très loin, il semble que le soleil et donc les destinations plus méridionales soient à la mode en 2010, ainsi que le dit Ken Faulkner, responsable du Travel Service du Caravan Club: «Le taux de change entre la livre et l’euro s’est stabilisé et les Anglais s’y sont habitués. Nos premières indications pour 2010 sont très bonnes. En janvier et février, qui sont des mois très importants pour nous, nous augmentons nos réservations à destination du continent de 15 à 20% par rapport à 2009.

Et la **France** demeure de loin la **destination favorite** de nos membres. Après le très mauvais temps qu’a connu l’Angleterre l’an passé, le soleil sera leur principale motivation.» Une analyse que reflète la presse spécialisée: «L’an passé fut une année difficile car il a fallu que nos concitoyens digèrent la dévaluation de la livre face à l’euro, admet Nigel Donnely, rédacteur en chef du magazine Practical Motorhome. Toutefois, comme nous le répétons souvent à nos lecteurs, même si nous avons perdu un peu de pouvoir d’achat dans la zone euro, partir en vacances en France demeure bon marché pour les Britanniques.D’autant que les **compagnies de ferries** ont fait de gros efforts pour rendre les traversées abordables. Beaucoup plus de gens nous parlent de la France cette année et si l’an passé les gens ne souhaitaient pas s’éloigner des ports d’arrivée des ferries, cette année les gens devraient voyager plus loin. Avec notre magazine, par exemple, nous organisons deux rallies qui conduiront nos lecteurs en Bourgogne ou dans le sud de la France.» Cet optimisme se concrétise dans les chiffres puisque les fabricants de caravanes sont heureux d’un salon avec des ventes en hausse par rapport à 2009 et qui complètent le très gros succès du salon d’octobre.De son côté, l’éditeur de guide et agent de Camping Cheque pour le Royaume-Uni, Alan Rogers, annonce une**hausse des ventes** de guides de 65% et une augmentation des ventes de camping chèques de 46% et confirme également un regain d’intérêt pour la France. Tous les indicateurs étant au beau fixe, il reste à espérer que les prochains mois confirmeront les espoirs qu’aura suscité le début d’année.

Le salon s’est en effet tenu une semaine plus tard que l’an passé et ne coïncidait donc pas avec les vacances scolaires anglaises et la météo n’a pas aidé à mobiliser les foules, avec de la neige les premiers jours et l’avis de tempête du 28 février pour la dernière journée. Si l’on ajoute à cela que la participation d’Aston Villa, club de football de Birmingham, à la finale de Coupe de la Ligue le dimanche après-midi aura retenu nombre de visiteurs potentiels devant la télévision, il faut admettre que la légère baisse de fréquentation du salon ne reflète pas du tout la popularité du camping chez nos voisins d’outre-Manche.
texts.1: La **grande question**pour les campings français était de savoir si les clients anglais allaient retrouver le chemin de la France après l’avoir boudée l’été dernier. Le salon de la caravane de Birmingham qui se tient en octobre avait donné des signes encourageants qui demandaient à être confirmés. Et ce fut le cas. Les visiteurs du salon ont montré une réelle envie de venir en France. Et si la tendance 2009 était de ne pas partir très loin, il semble que le soleil et donc les destinations plus méridionales soient à la mode en 2010, ainsi que le dit Ken Faulkner, responsable du Travel Service du Caravan Club: «Le taux de change entre la livre et l’euro s’est stabilisé et les Anglais s’y sont habitués. Nos premières indications pour 2010 sont très bonnes. En janvier et février, qui sont des mois très importants pour nous, nous augmentons nos réservations à destination du continent de 15 à 20% par rapport à 2009.
texts.2: Et la **France** demeure de loin la **destination favorite** de nos membres. Après le très mauvais temps qu’a connu l’Angleterre l’an passé, le soleil sera leur principale motivation.» Une analyse que reflète la presse spécialisée: «L’an passé fut une année difficile car il a fallu que nos concitoyens digèrent la dévaluation de la livre face à l’euro, admet Nigel Donnely, rédacteur en chef du magazine Practical Motorhome. Toutefois, comme nous le répétons souvent à nos lecteurs, même si nous avons perdu un peu de pouvoir d’achat dans la zone euro, partir en vacances en France demeure bon marché pour les Britanniques.D’autant que les **compagnies de ferries** ont fait de gros efforts pour rendre les traversées abordables. Beaucoup plus de gens nous parlent de la France cette année et si l’an passé les gens ne souhaitaient pas s’éloigner des ports d’arrivée des ferries, cette année les gens devraient voyager plus loin. Avec notre magazine, par exemple, nous organisons deux rallies qui conduiront nos lecteurs en Bourgogne ou dans le sud de la France.» Cet optimisme se concrétise dans les chiffres puisque les fabricants de caravanes sont heureux d’un salon avec des ventes en hausse par rapport à 2009 et qui complètent le très gros succès du salon d’octobre.De son côté, l’éditeur de guide et agent de Camping Cheque pour le Royaume-Uni, Alan Rogers, annonce une**hausse des ventes** de guides de 65% et une augmentation des ventes de camping chèques de 46% et confirme également un regain d’intérêt pour la France. Tous les indicateurs étant au beau fixe, il reste à espérer que les prochains mois confirmeront les espoirs qu’aura suscité le début d’année.

# The wonders of arthoscopic surgery will enable two Miami...
NEW ORLEANS --  The wonders of arthoscopic surgery will enable two Miami Hurricane starters to be ready for the Sugar Bowl Jan. 1 a month after suffering knee injuries.
Left guard Dave Alenka and linebacker Winston Moss injured their knees Nov. 30 in the Hurricanes' 58-7 victory over Notre Dame.
Both had arthoscopic surgery performed three days later.
Both are practicing this week and slated to start against Tennessee in the Sugar Bowl.
The officials for the Sugar Bowl will come from the Southwest Athletic Conference.
Wendell Shelton will be the referee and Joe Darden the umpire, Ken Faulkner, the supervisor of SWC Football Officials, announced.
The rest of the officiating crew is: Buddy Coleman, linesmen; Don George, line judge; George Sladky, field judge; Beau Hicks, side judge; Ron Murphy, back judge; and Walt Coleman is the alternate.
Buddy Coleman, Sladky and Murphy worked last year's Sugar Bowl.
The Miami team will participate in two parties while they are in New Orleans.
On Saturday, the team will be aboard the paddle boat Creole Queen and on Dec. 30, the Hurricanes will have a Mardi Gras party at a local hotel.
Both parties are restricted to the team and officials.

Title: Ken Faulkner - General

### Biography
After 34 years of following players and plays up and down football fields, blowing whistles and calling penalties, Ken Faulkner finally hung up his stripes for the last time on November 27, 1982. The game was Rice vs. Houston, two of his native state favorites. It was while working that game that Faulkner broke his ankle.
That injury, 12 years ago, took him off the field, but not away from college football. He still had his other love, serving as business manager of the Southwest Conference. When he finally retired in 1991, he also stepped down as SWC supervisor of football officials, a responsibility he handled for eight years.
When it comes to football, Ken Faulkner's dedication and devotion have made him a true "Legend of the Southwest" in officiating circles. Ask his SWC colleagues. To a man they'll tell you Faulkner made "a great impact on every football person he has ever worked with. He attracted enormous respect".
That respect has brought him recognition from the entire amateur football community and today he is honored by the National Football Foundation for his many years of work and contributions to the game.
Last year, Faulkner was similarly honored by the Collegiate Commissioners Association which presented him with its 1993 Football Officials Award of Merit.
During Faulkner's tenure as business manager, the Southwest Conference enjoyed a period of growth and athletic success unparalleled in the Conference's history. He oversaw distribution of Conference revenues for its nine member institutions which had combined to win 40 NCAA championships in 12 different sports during his nine-year watch. He managed $9 million annually for the SWC while, at the same time, supervising a crew of 40 officials.
Faulkner officiated his first football game while he was himself still a college student at what is today known as Mideastern State in Wichita Falls, Texas.
Faulkner said, "I discovered it was fun, something I really enjoyed." So he kept on doing it, even after he graduated with his bachelor's degree in physical education in 1950. Faulkner then got a job working for a freight company. But he kept those stripes and cleats clean for the weekend.

### Biography
As he progressed in his professional life, he was also stepping up on the gridiron. From officiating small college games, he graduated to larger ones and, finally, he was working major college games, some of the biggest games college football offered.
Among the Bowl Games Faulkner worked were the Orange, Sugar and Fiesta. He also regularly officiated one of college football's great rivalries, Texas versus Oklahoma.
In his off-the-field pursuits, Faulkner was a very successful major corporation internal auditor for 25 years. Then, in 1982, he joined the Southwest Conference as business manager. For Faulkner it was a perfect union of professional and personal pleasure.
Faulkner also became very involved in the work of the Collegiate Commissioners Association. For eight years he headed the CCA group that drafted and published officiating guidelines for the country's more than 10,000 college football officials.
These manuals deal with the mechanics of the job. "They tell the official everything he has to do from the time he gets out of his car at the stadium to the time he gets back home," says Faulkner. In addition to writing and producing the guidelines, Faulkner organized the distribution system to get them out to the officials all across the nation.
"That was midnight oil stuff," he says, "in addition to my duties with the Conference." And with no small amount of pride, he adds, "The system I set up is still in effect today."
Even though he officially retired in 1991, Faulkner is still involved in football. One of the things he does is scout college games, assessing officials who might be candidates to work for the National Football League.

**Kenneth Gordon Faulkner** (10 September 1923 – 2000) was an English footballer who played in the Football League for [Birmingham City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_F.C. "Birmingham City F.C.").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-3)

Faulkner was born in Smethwick, Staffordshire. Capped by [England at schoolboy level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Schools'_Football_Association "English Schools' Football Association"), he had a successful trial with [Birmingham City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_F.C. "Birmingham City F.C.") during the Second World War.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-Matthews86-4) Faulkner, a forward, played for Birmingham in the 1944–45 season of wartime competition,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-5) and also made guest appearances for [Coventry City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_City_F.C. "Millwall F.C."). The last game of that season proved to be his last for the club;[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-7) he was released in the 1947 close season and joined [Oldbury United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldbury_United_F.C. **Tales from the Creek Podcast | Ken Faulkner (January 2026)**
Ken Faulkner was inducted into the Campbell Athletics Hall of Fame in 1999. A guard on some of Campbell's finest basketball teams in the late 1960s, Faulkner went on to become one of the greatest coaches in New Jersey high school basketball history.
Faulkner was a four-year starter for Coach Fred McCall's and Coach Danny Roberts' Fighting Camels. During his junior and senior years, he helped the club to back-to-back 20-win seasons and NAIA District 29 championships.
In 1970, the Camels won 24 games and advanced to the NAIA National Tournament.
Following graduation in 1970, Faulkner returned to his native New Jersey and began a teaching and coaching career. He was named varsity boys basketball coach at Burlington Township High School and went on to build one of the premier programs in the state. In 24 seasons as a head coach, Faulkner's clubs won 522 games, 11 conference titles, seven South Jersey crowns and three state championships. His 1987 team posted a 31-0 record and is still considered one of the greatest teams in South Jersey basketball history.
Faulkner received numerous honors during his career. He was inducted into the Riverside High School, South Jersey Coaches, New Jersey Coaches and Basketball Club of South Jersey Halls of Fame. He was also presented the New Jersey Interscholastic Coaches Association's Honor Award.
Faulkner, who retired from coaching in 1996, later served in the New Jersey General Assembly.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
**Kenneth William Faulkner** (born 1948) is a former Republican Party politician who served for 10 weeks in the New Jersey General Assembly. After a collegiate career with the Campbell Fighting Camels basketball team, he was inducted into the Campbell University Hall of Fame.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-1) He is also a retired teacher, school administrator and high school basketball coach.
Faulkner grew up in Delanco Township, New Jersey and graduated from Riverside High School as part of the class of 1966. After playing at Campbell College (now Campbell University), he became a high school basketball coach. During his 24-year coaching career at Burlington Township High School, Faulkner led the team to a 521–129 record and three NJSIAA Group I state championships. He stepped down from his position as coach in 1996 to take a post as principal of Thomas O. Hopkins Middle School, stating that he couldn't be both a basketball coach and an effective school administrator.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-2)
Faulkner, a resident of Delanco Township, was chosen to replace Carmine DeSopo on the Republican ticket for the [7th Legislative District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey's_7th_legislative_district "New Jersey's 7th legislative district"), together with George Williams running for the other Assembly seat and Diane Allen for Senate.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-3)

In the November 1997 general elections, Allen won the Senate seat, while Democrats Herb Conaway and Jack Conners were declared the winners in that year's Assembly race, after a recount which showed that Conaway was the top vote-getter and Conners winning the second seat by a margin of 74 votes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-4) In September 1998, the New Jersey Superior Court threw out the results of the 1997 election due to problems with 160 uncounted ballots from a voting machine that affected the results for the second seat; Democrat Conners was ordered to leave office and Republican Faulkner was seated in his place.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-5)
The Republican committees of Burlington County and Camden County chose Faulkner to fill the vacated Assembly seat and the ballot position for the forthcoming special election; After being sworn into office on September 18, Faulkner used his first day in office to co-sponsor a bill raising awareness regarding arthritis, in addition to working to address issues related to education, healthcare and property taxes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-6)
In a November 1998 special election held based on the court order throwing out the 1997 election results, Conners defeated Faulkner by 5,500 votes and was sworn into office on November 23 for the second time that year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_William_Faulkner#cite_note-8)

### Biography
After 34 years of following players and plays up and down football fields, blowing whistles and calling penalties, Ken Faulkner finally hung up his stripes for the last time on November 27, 1982. The game was Rice vs. Houston, two of his native state favorites. It was while working that game that Faulkner broke his ankle.
That injury, 12 years ago, took him off the field, but not away from college football. He still had his other love, serving as business manager of the Southwest Conference. When he finally retired in 1991, he also stepped down as SWC supervisor of football officials, a responsibility he handled for eight years.
When it comes to football, Ken Faulkner's dedication and devotion have made him a true "Legend of the Southwest" in officiating circles. Ask his SWC colleagues. To a man they'll tell you Faulkner made "a great impact on every football person he has ever worked with. He attracted enormous respect".
That respect has brought him recognition from the entire amateur football community and today he is honored by the National Football Foundation for his many years of work and contributions to the game.
Last year, Faulkner was similarly honored by the Collegiate Commissioners Association which presented him with its 1993 Football Officials Award of Merit.
During Faulkner's tenure as business manager, the Southwest Conference enjoyed a period of growth and athletic success unparalleled in the Conference's history. He oversaw distribution of Conference revenues for its nine member institutions which had combined to win 40 NCAA championships in 12 different sports during his nine-year watch. He managed $9 million annually for the SWC while, at the same time, supervising a crew of 40 officials.
Faulkner officiated his first football game while he was himself still a college student at what is today known as Mideastern State in Wichita Falls, Texas.
Faulkner said, "I discovered it was fun, something I really enjoyed." So he kept on doing it, even after he graduated with his bachelor's degree in physical education in 1950. Faulkner then got a job working for a freight company. But he kept those stripes and cleats clean for the weekend.
texts.1:
### Biography
As he progressed in his professional life, he was also stepping up on the gridiron. From officiating small college games, he graduated to larger ones and, finally, he was working major college games, some of the biggest games college football offered.
Among the Bowl Games Faulkner worked were the Orange, Sugar and Fiesta. He also regularly officiated one of college football's great rivalries, Texas versus Oklahoma.
In his off-the-field pursuits, Faulkner was a very successful major corporation internal auditor for 25 years. Then, in 1982, he joined the Southwest Conference as business manager. For Faulkner it was a perfect union of professional and personal pleasure.
Faulkner also became very involved in the work of the Collegiate Commissioners Association. For eight years he headed the CCA group that drafted and published officiating guidelines for the country's more than 10,000 college football officials.
These manuals deal with the mechanics of the job. "They tell the official everything he has to do from the time he gets out of his car at the stadium to the time he gets back home," says Faulkner. In addition to writing and producing the guidelines, Faulkner organized the distribution system to get them out to the officials all across the nation.
"That was midnight oil stuff," he says, "in addition to my duties with the Conference." And with no small amount of pride, he adds, "The system I set up is still in effect today."
Even though he officially retired in 1991, Faulkner is still involved in football. One of the things he does is scout college games, assessing officials who might be candidates to work for the National Football League.

Aston Villa have confirmed that Paul Faulkner has stepped down as chief executive.
Faulkner’s departure continues a summer of upheaval at the Midlands club, with owner Randy Lerner currently looking for a buyer after putting Villa up for sale.
There have also been changes in manager Paul Lambert’s backroom as Roy Keane became his new assistant after the sackings of previous No 2 Ian Culverhouse and head of football operations Gary Karsa.

# Emery is a 'magician' - former Villa chief executive
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Unai Emery
By
Nick Mashiter in Istanbul
Football reporter
*   Published 20 May 2026
**Former****Aston Villa****chief executive Paul Faulkner has labelled Unai Emery a "magician".**
The Villa boss took over when the club was three points above the relegation zone in November 2022 before taking them into Europe by the end of the season.
He has guided Villa to the Champions League twice, having sealed a second qualification last week after beating Liverpool, and is on the brink of ending the club's 30-year trophy drought in Istanbul.
"He's been incredible as a manager. The team was struggling under his predecessor, Steven Gerrard, and he's just transformed it," said Faulkner, who was chief executive under former owner Randy Lerner for four years.
"He's got a lot of the same players, they've added a little bit to the squad but a lot of this team have been there for an awfully long time, predating the manager.
"You see how he's managed to knit that unit together and get consistent results. Absolutely remarkable, I think he's a magician.
"It would be nice now just to cap that off with some silverware. These opportunities are tough to get to so when you are in a final it'll be great to get the tangible return on the brilliant work he's done."

**Kenneth Gordon Faulkner** (10 September 1923 – 2000) was an English footballer who played in the Football League for [Birmingham City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_F.C. "Birmingham City F.C.").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-3)

Faulkner was born in Smethwick, Staffordshire. Capped by [England at schoolboy level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Schools'_Football_Association "English Schools' Football Association"), he had a successful trial with [Birmingham City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_F.C. "Birmingham City F.C.") during the Second World War.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-Matthews86-4) Faulkner, a forward, played for Birmingham in the 1944–45 season of wartime competition,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-5) and also made guest appearances for [Coventry City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_City_F.C. "Coventry City F.C.") and [Port Vale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Vale_F.C. "Port Vale F.C.").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-6) He made his debut in the penultimate game of the 1946–47 Second Division season, playing at outside right in a 2–0 win at [Millwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millwall_F.C. "Millwall F.C."). The last game of that season proved to be his last for the club;[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-7) he was released in the 1947 close season and joined [Oldbury United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldbury_United_F.C. "Oldbury United F.C.").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Faulkner#cite_note-Matthews86-4)

# Paul Faulkner
Paul Faulkner is the Co-Founder of Element45, an advisory business that works with a range of clients providing Board-level support and leadership services.
Prior to this Paul has held roles as Chief Executive of Aston Villa and Nottingham Forest Football Clubs, as well as being CEO of the Greater Birmingham Chambers of Commerce and Chief of Staff for the Richardson family business.
Outside of work Paul is a Trustee of Kids’ Village, a charity aiming to build the UK’s first holiday village offering respite breaks to sick children and their families. He has previously held pro-bono roles as Chair of Sport Birmingham, Vice-Chair of Town Hall Symphony Hall Birmingham and Trustee of Cure Leukaemia, Birmingham Children’s Hospital Charity and the Lord Mayor of Birmingham’s Charity.
In 2024 he received the award of ‘Brummie of the Year’.
Paul lives in Sutton Coldfield and is married with two young sons.

# Paul Faulkner
Paul Faulkner is the Co-Founder of Element45, an advisory business that works with a range of clients providing Board-level support and leadership services.
Prior to this Paul has held roles as Chief Executive of Aston Villa and Nottingham Forest Football Clubs, as well as being CEO of the Greater Birmingham Chambers of Commerce and Chief of Staff for the Richardson family business.
Outside of work Paul is a Trustee of Kids’ Village, a charity aiming to build the UK’s first holiday village offering respite breaks to sick children and their families. He has previously held pro-bono roles as Chair of Sport Birmingham, Vice-Chair of Town Hall Symphony Hall Birmingham and Trustee of Cure Leukaemia, Birmingham Children’s Hospital Charity and the Lord Mayor of Birmingham’s Charity.
In 2024 he received the award of ‘Brummie of the Year’.
Paul lives in Sutton Coldfield and is married with two young sons.

Aston Villa have confirmed that Paul Faulkner has stepped down as chief executive.
Faulkner’s departure continues a summer of upheaval at the Midlands club, with owner Randy Lerner currently looking for a buyer after putting Villa up for sale.
There have also been changes in manager Paul Lambert’s backroom as Roy Keane became his new assistant after the sackings of previous No 2 Ian Culverhouse and head of football operations Gary Karsa.

# Emery is a 'magician' - former Villa chief executive
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Unai Emery
By
Nick Mashiter in Istanbul
Football reporter
*   Published 20 May 2026
**Former****Aston Villa****chief executive Paul Faulkner has labelled Unai Emery a "magician".**
The Villa boss took over when the club was three points above the relegation zone in November 2022 before taking them into Europe by the end of the season.
He has guided Villa to the Champions League twice, having sealed a second qualification last week after beating Liverpool, and is on the brink of ending the club's 30-year trophy drought in Istanbul.
"He's been incredible as a manager. The team was struggling under his predecessor, Steven Gerrard, and he's just transformed it," said Faulkner, who was chief executive under former owner Randy Lerner for four years.
"He's got a lot of the same players, they've added a little bit to the squad but a lot of this team have been there for an awfully long time, predating the manager.
"You see how he's managed to knit that unit together and get consistent results. Absolutely remarkable, I think he's a magician.
"It would be nice now just to cap that off with some silverware. These opportunities are tough to get to so when you are in a final it'll be great to get the tangible return on the brilliant work he's done."

### The EFL Championship Era
[edit]
After being relegated in 2011, Birmingham are still yet to gain promotion back to the top flight of English football. However, since Alex McLeish was sacked as Villa manager, Villa's poor form continued. Despite several manager changes over the next few years, after several close calls they were finally relegated at the end of the 2015/16 season. Earlier on in the 2015/16 season, the two teams were drawn to play each other in the third round of the League Cup. Aston Villa ran out 1–0 winners thanks to a goal from Rudy Gestede. In the 2016–17 season the two teams faced off in the second tier of English football for the first time since 1987. The first game at St Andrew's ended in a 1–1 draw. Villa won the second match 1–0 with a 69th-minute goal scored by Agbonlahor. The two sides faced each other again in the league during the 2017/18 season, producing a 0–0 draw at St. Andrews, marred by Birmingham fans throwing clappers at the Villa players all throughout the game,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-27) before Villa achieved a 2–0 victory in front of 41,232 spectators at Villa Park with lifelong Villa fan and local Jack Grealish, who produced a match-winning man-of-the-match display. The teams next met on 25 November 2018 in one of the most exciting derby games in recent times, Villa ran out 4–2 winners after goals from Jonathan Kodjia, Jack Grealish, a Tammy Abraham penalty and Alan Hutton who ran half the length of the pitch to score, Pedersen and Lukas Jutkiewicz scored for Birmingham.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-28)

### The EFL Championship Era
On 10 March 2019, a Birmingham City fan invaded the pitch during the return fixture at St. Andrew's and assaulted Aston Villa captain Jack Grealish on the pitch by punching him from behind in the head, which was labelled as "disgraceful and cowardly" by supporters of both teams. The man was arrested and charged by West Midlands Police. Later that month, the attacker, 27-year-old Paul Mitchell, was convicted of assault and encroachment onto a football pitch at Birmingham Magistrates Court and jailed for 14 weeks, receiving £350 of fines and a 10-year ban from all football stadiums.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-29) Mitchell died in 2023 of a drug overdose.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-30) St Andrew's' security was criticised as a result. The game ended in an ironic twist with a 1–0 win for Aston Villa with Grealish scoring the winning goal.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-32) At the end of the same season, Villa were promoted as they won ten in a row including that game. Since then, this fiercely contested fixture hasn't been played between the two rivals.

### The EFL Championship Era
[Birmingham City W.F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_W.F.C. "Birmingham City W.F.C.") were founded in 1968, whilst [Aston Villa W.F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Villa_W.F.C. "Aston Villa W.F.C.") were founded in 1973 as Solihull F.C., and took on their current Aston Villa guise in 1996. During the [2000-01](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000%E2%80%9301_FA_Women's_Premier_League "2000–01 FA Women's Premier League") and [2001-02](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001%E2%80%9302_FA_Women's_Premier_League "2001–02 FA Women's Premier League") seasons both teams competed in the second tier FA Women's Premier League North. Birmingham were then promoted to the Women's Premier League National with Villa joining them for one season in [2003-04](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003%E2%80%9304_FA_Women's_Premier_League "2003–04 FA Women's Premier League") before being relegated. Then followed 18 years of the teams being in different divisions, Birmingham being in the top tier and Villa elsewhere, until the 2020–21 Women's Super League season when Villa were promoted up to join Blues. In the first ever WSL match between the two sides Birmingham beat Villa 1–0 at an empty Villa Park (due to restrictions related to the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom),[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-33) while the Birmingham's home match which was also played behind closed doors at Damson Park, Solihull was a 1–1 draw.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-34) In the 2021–22 season, Aston Villa won 1–0 at St.

### The EFL Championship Era

In the 2026–27 stadium, Birmingham City had earned promotion and both teams were once again in the WSL. texts.10:
### The EFL Championship Era
[edit]
After being relegated in 2011, Birmingham are still yet to gain promotion back to the top flight of English football. However, since Alex McLeish was sacked as Villa manager, Villa's poor form continued. Despite several manager changes over the next few years, after several close calls they were finally relegated at the end of the 2015/16 season. Earlier on in the 2015/16 season, the two teams were drawn to play each other in the third round of the League Cup. Aston Villa ran out 1–0 winners thanks to a goal from Rudy Gestede. In the 2016–17 season the two teams faced off in the second tier of English football for the first time since 1987. The first game at St Andrew's ended in a 1–1 draw. Villa won the second match 1–0 with a 69th-minute goal scored by Agbonlahor. The two sides faced each other again in the league during the 2017/18 season, producing a 0–0 draw at St. Andrews, marred by Birmingham fans throwing clappers at the Villa players all throughout the game,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-27) before Villa achieved a 2–0 victory in front of 41,232 spectators at Villa Park with lifelong Villa fan and local Jack Grealish, who produced a match-winning man-of-the-match display. The teams next met on 25 November 2018 in one of the most exciting derby games in recent times, Villa ran out 4–2 winners after goals from Jonathan Kodjia, Jack Grealish, a Tammy Abraham penalty and Alan Hutton who ran half the length of the pitch to score, Pedersen and Lukas Jutkiewicz scored for Birmingham.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-28)
texts.11:
### The EFL Championship Era
On 10 March 2019, a Birmingham City fan invaded the pitch during the return fixture at St. Andrew's and assaulted Aston Villa captain Jack Grealish on the pitch by punching him from behind in the head, which was labelled as "disgraceful and cowardly" by supporters of both teams. The man was arrested and charged by West Midlands Police. Later that month, the attacker, 27-year-old Paul Mitchell, was convicted of assault and encroachment onto a football pitch at Birmingham Magistrates Court and jailed for 14 weeks, receiving £350 of fines and a 10-year ban from all football stadiums.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-29) Mitchell died in 2023 of a drug overdose.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-30) St Andrew's' security was criticised as a result. The game ended in an ironic twist with a 1–0 win for Aston Villa with Grealish scoring the winning goal.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-32) At the end of the same season, Villa were promoted as they won ten in a row including that game. Since then, this fiercely contested fixture hasn't been played between the two rivals.

### The EFL Championship Era
As of the 2026–27 season, Birmingham currently play at [St Andrew's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Andrew's_(stadium) "St Andrew's (stadium)"), home of the men's team, having played at [Redditch Utd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redditch_United_F.C. ## Statistics and records
[edit]
As of the end of the 2018–19 season, there have been 126 meetings in major competition between the two teams since the first FA Cup meeting in 1887, of which Aston Villa have won 57 and Birmingham City 38.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-soccer-39) The most goals in one game were scored in a league game on 7 July 1895, in the First Division, as Small Heath lost to Aston Villa 7–3.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-soccer-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-SG-40) The biggest winning margin was 6–0 to Aston Villa on 9 November 1988, in a Full Members Cup fixture.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-soccer-39)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-41) The last Birmingham City league victory over Aston Villa was on 20 March 2005, when Blues won 2–0 at St Andrew's. Villa won six encounters in a row following this and have remained unbeaten in 14 league encounters. The two teams drew for the first time in over six years in the next match (the first of three in the 2010–11 season), with the match finishing 0–0 (the other Premier League match of the season also finished as a draw). The second match of the season resulted in the first Blues derby win since 2005, as they beat Villa 2–1 in the 2010–11 League Cup Quarter Final on 1 December 2010.

[edit]
As of the end of the 2018–19 season, there have been 126 meetings in major competition between the two teams since the first FA Cup meeting in 1887, of which Aston Villa have won 57 and Birmingham City 38.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-soccer-39) The most goals in one game were scored in a league game on 7 July 1895, in the First Division, as Small Heath lost to Aston Villa 7–3.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-soccer-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-SG-40) The biggest winning margin was 6–0 to Aston Villa on 9 November 1988, in a Full Members Cup fixture.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-soccer-39)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_derby#cite_note-41) The last Birmingham City league victory over Aston Villa was on 20 March 2005, when Blues won 2–0 at St Andrew's. Villa won six encounters in a row following this and have remained unbeaten in 14 league encounters. The two teams drew for the first time in over six years in the next match (the first of three in the 2010–11 season), with the match finishing 0–0 (the other Premier League match of the season also finished as a draw). The second match of the season resulted in the first Blues derby win since 2005, as they beat Villa 2–1 in the 2010–11 League Cup Quarter Final on 1 December 2010.

### Women's Sides
[Birmingham City W.F.C.](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/Birmingham_City_W.F.C. "Birmingham City W.F.C.") were founded in 1968, whilst [Aston Villa W.F.C.](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/Aston_Villa_W.F.C. "Aston Villa W.F.C.") were founded in 1973 as Solihull F.C., and took on their current Aston Villa guise in 1996. During the [2000-01](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/2000%E2%80%9301_FA_Women's_Premier_League "2000–01 FA Women's Premier League") and [2001-02](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/2001%E2%80%9302_FA_Women's_Premier_League "2001–02 FA Women's Premier League") seasons both teams competed in the second tier FA Women's Premier League North. Birmingham were then promoted to the Women's Premier League National with Villa joining them for one season in [2003-04](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/2003%E2%80%9304_FA_Women's_Premier_League "2003–04 FA Women's Premier League") before being relegated. Then followed 18 years of the teams being in different divisions, Birmingham being in the top tier and Villa elsewhere, until the 2020–21 Women's Super League season when Villa were promoted up to join Blues. In the first ever WSL match between the two sides Birmingham beat Villa 1–0 at an empty Villa Park (due to restrictions related to the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom),[[33]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/Second_City_derby#cite_note-33) while the Birmingham's home match which was also played behind closed doors at Damson Park, Solihull was a 1–1 draw.[[34]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/Second_City_derby#cite_note-34) In the 2021–22 season, Aston Villa won 1–0 at St.

Ken Faulkner (who played for Birmingham City in the 1940s) was a member of **Birmingham City** – the club that last defeated the league’s 1894‑95 FA Cup winner, Aston Villa, on **20 March 2005** when the Blues won 2–0 at St Andrew’s.
